title: the best of 2008: hearing science
display_name: The Best of 2008: Hearing Science
abstract: the world of hearing science continues to produce excitement discovering new genes and increasing understanding of those genes that we already knew a little about, gaining deeper insight into what happens to sound after it leaves the ear and how brain processing can change over time, understanding why some people are more affected by exposure to noise than others, and so on. these are some of the topics that a review of the hearing science literature found in our audiology journals in 2008. view them as, perhaps, just teasers that will then lead you to other topics and studies that appear in a vast array of scientific journals ranging from the journal of the association for research in otolaryngology to hearing research to the journal of the acoustical society of america to human molecular genetics to the journal of neuroscience to... well, you get the picture. what follows are just a few of the many excellent articles that i read in the audiology journals this past year. as always, i join with drs. mueller, stach, and wark and welcome dr. zeng to our group in commending all the 2008 authors for their excellent contributions to the audiology literature. great for the clinician research changes clinical practice and, as with the articles selected here, increases our knowledge base with information that helps us interpret test results and manage hearing problems. the first of these relates to genetics and hearing loss, an area that is constantly changing. not only are new genes identified, but we are also learning about interactions among genes, and, of importance to our job, what characteristics and variations we might associate with various genetic mutations and genetic disorders. one example appeared in an article in the international journal of audiology (ija) by deepika gopalarao, william kimberling, walt jesteadt and their colleagues at boys town national research hospital. they asked whether or not progressive hearing loss occurs with the common 35delg mutation of the gjb2 (connexin 26) gene, a mutation that is typically (but not always) associated with severe-profound hearing loss. the authors note that in past studies, definitions of what constituted a change in hearing sometimes made it difficult to determine if progression had occurred. consistent with other reports, the authors found progressive loss in some homozygous 35delg mutation cases. particularly valuable parts of this article are a discussion of methods for tracking progression over time and a comprehensive summary of previous articles. with multiple groups using similar methods and guides for interpretation, we should be able to accumulate larger numbers and thus better understand what variation we can expect in our patients with hearing loss related to gjb2 mutations. moving from molecules to words, an article in the journal of the american academy of audiology (jaaa) by rachel mcardle and richard wilson examined factors that influence word-recognition performance in noise. these include acoustics, phonetic content of a word (voicing, manner, place information), and lexical information (word frequency, familiarity, etc.). drawing on the data from a companion article, the authors examined a large corpus of responses and found that acoustic and phonetic information accounted for most of the variability in performance. this points to the acoustic properties of words as the foundation for speech perception and a bottom-up type of processing. the authors suggest that in evaluating pre- and post-intervention performance, as with amplification, while sentences have higher face validity, words may be more sensitive to acoustic changes without the influence of lexical confounds. as clinicians, we must think about what we want to know and then use the best methods words for certain applications and sentences for others. information like that contained in this article should help us with that decision. my third selection was written by yvonne sininger and stella de bode and published in ear and hearing. they report on a study in which they examined right-left ear asymmetry in temporal processing in listeners with normal hearing and subjects with unilateral deafness. results showed the expected right-ear advantage for gap detection when a noise stimulus was used and a smaller left-ear advantage in gap detection for tonal signals in subjects with normal hearing. many questions remain about the effects of unilateral hearing loss and whether it leads to any form of central compensation. here, listeners with unilateral deafness demonstrated performance in their hearing ear similar to that of the normal-hearing subjects. as we continue to explore and characterize the effects of mild and unilateral hearing losses, well-constructed studies like this should be very helpful. best quick read it can be difficult to find a quick read in hearing science. i've come up with a couple articles that fit this category and i'll try to convince you that the third one might qualify as a quick read. the first article comes from e. a. da costa, j.c. castro, and i.e. macedo in brazil. writing in ija, they revisit the possibility (and sometimes controversy) of a relationship between pigmentation and susceptibility to noise-induced hearing loss. they compared iris color and audiometric thresholds in a retrospective study that involved 2787 workers employed from 1993 2003, with 2407 of these workers exposed to high noise levels. what makes this article particularly interesting is not only the number of subjects but that all participants were employed at the same metalwork facility. the authors found that fair-eyed noise-exposed workers had high-frequency thresholds that were 8-10 db poorer than their dark-eyed co-workers, while non-noise-exposed workers at the facility showed no differences between eye color groups. these findings reinforce the importance of ear protection for this fair-eyed writer! the next article, published in ear and hearing, is also on noise exposure, but this time on prevention. po-wen cheng, shing-hwa lin, yi-ho young, and their colleagues in taiwan report on an investigation of attenuation of noise-induced hearing loss by d-methionine in an effort to elucidate biochemical changes in atpase activities and oxidative stress resulting from exposure to noise. in this study, guinea pigs were exposed to noise with half of the subjects treated with d-methionine and half with saline. it was found that noise influenced atpase activities and created oxidative stress in the cochlea and that the group given d-methionine displayed less threshold shift, faster recovery, and less adverse biochemical changes in the cochlea. my final quick read is about auditory cortex anatomy. while you may not think of neuroanatomy as a topic for a quick read, let me try to persuade you to put this important update on your reading list even if takes longer to read than some. would it help if i told you it's only five pages long? in a special issue of jaaa highlighting hearing research at vanderbilt university, my colleague troy hackett provides an overview of the current understanding of the anatomical organization of the auditory cortex. it is presented very clearly and concisely by a leader in this area of very difficult research. this article will give you an overview of a current working model of the functional organization of the human auditory cortex. this information provides an important context for studies, such as those addressing auditory processing, where relationships among anatomical, imaging, and electrophysiological data are discussed. not ready for pubmed i'll lead off this section by mentioning a useful and important article in the hearing journal by catherine palmer, elaine mormer, amanda ortman, and their colleagues that provides a practical set of guidelines for evaluating published articles, their value, and their clinical relevance. while they focus on evaluating evidence for clinical application, many of the lessons here apply to evaluating various types of research studies and applications. kudos to dr. palmer and her colleagues for building on a topic that robyn cox has discussed in her publications. brian moore of the university of cambridge, one of the most prolific contributors to the hearing science literature, contrasts the roles of envelope and temporal fine structure in conveying speech information in an article in audiology today (at). in a must-read for clinicians, dr. moore argues that while envelope information has been regarded as important for speech signals in quiet, temporal fine structure plays a critical and important role in pitch perception, masking, and the perception of speech in noise. the article concludes with some reasons for considering temporal fine structure when thinking about amplification. a moment of science in at continues to provide insightful information on new developments in hearing science. in one entry in 2008, shimon francis and lisa cunningham discuss the mysteries of hair cell mechanotransduction, a big word that they skillfully demystify. we know quite a bit about the structure and organization of hair cells and stereocilia and their role in signal transduction. we know that bending of the stereocilia is related to the opening of mechanically gated transduction channels and we know some things about the proteins found in the inner ear. however, the mystery remains as to the molecular identity of the mechanotransduction channel. so, read the first few chapters now, then stay tuned to find out who (i.e., which molecule) done it. most thought provoking just about everything in hearing science is thought provoking, so i have a difficult time choosing from among so many interesting studies. you may have noticed that i've made it this far and have barely mentioned auditory evoked potentials. well, i just can't pass that topic up and, in fact, there are two articles related to cortical potentials that i'd like to bring to your attention. they grabbed my attention with their use of novel methods to explore speech processing and their ideas about possible applications of objective methods, especially in infants and children. in the first article, published in the journal of speech, language and hearing research, patrick wong, ajith uppunda, todd parrish, and sumitrajit dhar explore cortical mechanisms of speech perception in noise using fmri. when they compared responses to speech in quiet to those for easy and difficult noise conditions, the researchers found that listening to speech in noise activates a network of brain areas more complex than what is seen in quiet. these data show increased activation in areas of the superior temporal gyrus in noise as well as other areas of cortex. these results further support the importance of additional processes, such as attention and cognition, in understanding the ability to process speech in noise. as we learn from this study and the next how the normal system works, we gain a foundation for understanding what happens when a system is not working correctly, as in the situation of incomplete or compromised development. another interesting article about cortical responses to speech stimuli appeared in ear and hearing. most studies that record evoked potentials use brief stimuli or, in the case of speech, speech syllables or monosyllabic words. using a cleverly conceived approach, steven aiken and terence picton obtained cortical responses to sentences. when they compared the envelope of the sentence stimulus to the cortical evoked potential, they showed that the human auditory cortical response follows the envelope of a speech sentence or represents the transient characteristics of the envelope. this article broadens possibilities in evaluating neural representation of speech and may eventually help us understand basic function as well as the effectiveness of various forms of intervention. the final article for this category, published in jaaa, explores the area of speech perception in noise from a behavioral perspective. andrew stuart reports on reception thresholds for sentences in quiet, continuous noise, and interrupted noise in normal school-aged children. this study caught my attention as we try to understand similarities and differences between children and adults in processing speech in noise. he found that children require more favorable signal-to-noise ratios than adults, but show similar benefit from interrupted over continuous competing noise. the author suggests that comparison of sentence recognition in interrupted versus continuous noise has potential as a clinical tool to assess temporal processing ability in young children. if so, clinicians would have another useful approach when evaluating auditory abilities in children. all-around favorite i have two all-around favorites this year (yes, it's always difficult to settle on just one). one is an ear & hearing article in which john rosowski, hideko nakajima, and saumil merchant describe the clinical utility of laser-doppler vibrometer, or ldv, measurements in live normal and pathologic human ears. ldv is a method that allows measurement of velocity of the tympanic membrane near the umbo. the investigators demonstrate that ldv is both sensitive and selective for the differentiation of various ossicular disorders and is also sensitive to pathology involving inner ear sound conduction, such as superior semicircular canal dehiscence. the very thorough description of the technique and presentations of ldv findings for various types of abnormal ears, such as ossicular interruption or malleus fixation, provide a comprehensive view of interest to researchers and clinicians alike. i enjoyed learning more about this topic, and particularly thinking about how it might be a new tool to refine clinical diagnosis of conductive hearing problems. my other favorite, also in e&h, is by jos eggermont, who discusses various effects of sound on auditory cortical plasticity. this review of work from his and other lab groups highlights changes in neural representation in the auditory cortex that can occur throughout the life span, though effects may differ between children and adults. there are several interesting aspects to this review, a reflection of the breadth and creativity of dr. eggermont's research. first, plasticity occurring during maturation has benefit in allowing adaptation related to deafness and introduction of sound through hearing aids or cochlear implants. on the other hand, changes in cortical representation of frequency as a result of hearing loss may have an adverse effect, such as tinnitus. an especially interesting aspect of this discussion is presentation of evidence showing that exposure to an enhanced acoustic environment, made up of moderate sound levels that don't themselves lead to hearing loss, still can lead to changes in cortical tonotopic maps. conclusion it was another year of great articles published in our audiology journals, and i've mentioned only a few. to the researchers and authors, keep writing, and to all of us, keep reading. hearing science offers a lot of gems that enhance our understanding and clinical practice.

abstract: the 2023 padua days of muscle and mobility medicine (pdm3) were held from march 29th to april 1st, 2023. most of the abstracts were published electronically in the european journal of translational myology (ejtm) 33 (1) 2023. here we report the complete book of abstracts that confirms the interest of more than 150 scientists and clinicians from austria, bulgaria, canada, denmark, france, georgia, germany, iceland, ireland, italy, mongolia, norway, russia, slovakia, slovenia, spain, switzerland, the netherlands and usa to gather to the hotel petrarca of thermae of euganean hills, padua, italy for contributing and attending the pdm3 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zc02d4upwrg). the 2023 pdm3 started march 29th in the historic aula guariento of thepadua galilean academy of letters, arts and sciences with the lecture of prof. carlo reggiani and ended in the late afternoon with the lecture of professor terje l mo after introductory words of professor stefano schiaffino. the program followed in the hotel petrarca conferenece halls from march 30 to april 1, 2023. the extended topic interests of specialists in basic myology sciences and clinicians, collected under the umbrella neologism of mobility medicine, is stressed also by expansion of sections of the ejtm editorial board (https://www.pagepressjournals.org/index.php/bam/board). we hope that speakers of the 2023 pdm3 and readers of ejtm will submit ejtm communications to the european journal of translational myology (pagepress, pavia, italy) by may 31, 2023 and/or invited review and original articles for the 2023 special issue: "pdm3" of diagnostics, mdpi, basel, switzerland due september 30, 2023.

title: vestibular hypofunction in patients with presbycusis: a cross-sectional study
display_name: Vestibular Hypofunction in Patients with Presbycusis: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: background: vestibular hypofunction (vh) and hearing loss can affect quality of life and lead to disability, especially in the elderly. studies investigating presbycusis and vestibular function in the aging population have been conducted separately, but few have examined the combination of both conditions in older patients, with inconsistent results that may be due to small sample sizes or heterogeneity in the methods used to assess vestibular function. we aimed to characterize the occurrence of vh in patients with presbycusis using the video head impulse test (vhit), which is a specific and reliable assessment tool for vh. methods: a prospective, cross-sectional study of 200 individuals was conducted at hamad medical corporation-qatar in doha, qatar. adults aged 50 years and older with bilateral age-related hearing loss were screened for eligibility and those who were eligible completed the vhit. patient history, demographics, audiological and clinical data were collected. vh was defined as vestibulo-ocular reflex (vor) gain of <0.79 and presence of corrective saccades. results: in our study population, (n = 200 mean age 64.1 8.4 [range = 37], 31.5% females), vh was identified in 12 out of 200 patients (6.0%, 95% ci: 3.3 10.1) with bilateral age-related hearing loss (arhl), equivalent to approximately 1 in 17 patients. vh was detected in the left ear in 11 patients (5.5%, 95% ci: 2.9 9.9), the right ear in five patients (2.5%, 95% ci: 0.8 5.8), and bilaterally in four patients (2.0%, 95% ci: 0.6 5.4). conclusions: in our study population, vestibular hypofunction was observed in 6% of patients with bilateral symmetrical age-related sensorineural hearing loss, suggesting that vestibular screening may be useful in this population at risk.

title: the heterozygous p.a684v variant in the wfs1 gene is a mutational hotspot causing a severe hearing loss phenotype
display_name: The Heterozygous p.A684V Variant in the WFS1 Gene Is a Mutational Hotspot Causing a Severe Hearing Loss Phenotype

authorships.name: Norio Yamamoto
institutions: Kobe City Medical Center General Hospital

abstract: background/objectives: a heterozygous mutation in the wfs1 gene is responsible for autosomal dominant non-syndromic hearing loss (dfna6/14/38) and wolfram-like syndrome, which is characterized by bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with optic atrophy and/or diabetes mellitus. however, detailed clinical features for the patients with the heterozygous p.a684v variant remain unknown. methods: we report the clinical details of 14 cases with a heterozygous p.a684v variant in the wfs1 gene identified from target resequencing analysis of 63 previously reported deafness genes by next-generation sequencing of 15,684 hearing loss patients (mean age 27.5 23.1 years old, 6574 male, 8612 female and 498 for whom information was unavailable). results: among the 14 patients from 13 families with the p.a684v variant, nine were sporadic cases. in addition, we confirmed de novo occurrence of this variant in seven families. this result strongly supports the notion that this variant was located on a mutational hotspot. when comparing previously reported cases of autosomal dominant wfs1 gene-associated hearing loss, most of the patients in this study showed severe-to-profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (genotype phenotype correlation). two patients had optic atrophy, while the others did not have any other complications. conclusions: the identified heterozygous p.a684v variant appears to be a hotspot mutation and likely to cause severe-to-profound hearing loss in early childhood. cochlear implantation is considered favorable in cases of hearing impairment due to this variant.

title: interpreting pendred syndrome as a foetal hydrops: clinical and animal model evidence
display_name: Interpreting pendred syndrome as a foetal hydrops: Clinical and animal model evidence

authorships.name: François Simon
institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authorships.name: Mathieu Beraneck
institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

abstract: background: meni re disease (md) and slc26a4 related deafness (pendred syndrome (ps) or dfnb4) are two different inner ear disorders which present with fluctuating and progressive hearing loss, which could be a direct consequence of endolymphatic hydrops. objective: to present similarities between both pathologies and explore how the concept of hydrops may be applied to ps/dfnb4. methods: review of the literature on md, ps/dfnb4 and mouse model of ps/dfnb4. results: md and ps/dfnb4 share a number of similarities such as fluctuating and progressive hearing loss, acute episodes with vertigo and tinnitus, mri and histological evidence of endolymphatic hydrops (although with different underlying mechanisms). md is usually diagnosed during the fourth decade of life whereas ps/dfnb4 is congenital. the ps/dfnb4 mouse models have shown that biallelic slc26a4 mutations lead to na+ and water retention in the endolymph during the perinatal period, which in turn induces degeneration of the stria vascularis and hearing loss. crossing clinical/imagery characteristics and animal models, evidence seems to support the hypothesis of ps being a foetal hydrops. conclusions: when understanding ps/dfnb4 as a developmental hydrops, treatments used in md could be repositioned to ps.

title: genetic alterations in patients with nf2-related schwannomatosis and sporadic vestibular schwannomas
display_name: Genetic Alterations in Patients with NF2-Related Schwannomatosis and Sporadic Vestibular Schwannomas
abstract: background: unilateral (uvs) and bilateral vestibular schwannoma (bvs) are distinct disease types, yet share tumorigenic features. this study examined causative genetic alterations in three groups: patients with nf2-related schwannomatosis (nf2), young patients with uvs ( 30 years), and older patients with uvs ( 40 years). methods: lymphocyte and vestibular schwannoma dna was genetically analyzed. outcomes included gene involvement, pathogenicity classification, variant type, effect, and location, and loss of heterozygosity (loh) of chromosome 22. results: among 93 patients, 17% had nf2, 39% were 30 years with uvs, and 44% were 40 years with uvs. in all patients with nf2 (100%), two or more hits were detected in the tumor dna, whereas patients with uvs had a slightly lower detection rate (89 98%). nf2-related tumors had a higher frequency of nucleotide variants (76%), while loh events were more common in uvs (64 69%). variants were mostly identified in nf2, with nonsense variants over-represented in patients with nf2 (38%) and frameshift variants more prevalent in uvs (44 51%). conclusions: biallelic nf2 inactivation primarily drives vestibular schwannoma tumorigenesis. in patients with nf2, two pathogenic nf2 variants or one nf2 variant with loh are common, whereas patients with uvs often exhibit one nf2 variant with loh. additionally, variant types differ between patient groups.
